claim: The NeMo Platform Python SDK and CLI both support retrieving an auditor configuration by name and workspace.
premises: The Python code example uses client.audit.configs.retrieve with name='demo-basic-config' and workspace='default'
The CLI command example uses 'nmp audit configs get demo-basic-config --workspace default -f json'

claim: An auditor configuration contains structured sections for plugins, reporting, run parameters, and system settings.
premises: The example output shows top-level keys: plugins, reporting, run, and system
Each section contains specific configuration parameters relevant to its domain

claim: The demo-basic-config uses specific probe specifications including dan.AutoDANCached and goodside.Tag for vulnerability scanning.
premises: The plugins section shows probe_spec: 'dan.AutoDANCached,goodside.Tag'
The user_agent string references 'LLM vulnerability scanner https://garak.ai'

claim: The configuration enables parallel processing with 20 parallel attempts but disables parallel requests.
premises: The system section shows parallel_attempts: 20
The system section shows parallel_requests: false

claim: The auditor configuration includes metadata fields for tracking creation, updates, and workspace association.
premises: The output contains id, created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by, and workspace fields
Both example outputs show identical metadata structure with different entity IDs

claim: A Model Entity in NeMo Platform serves as a model card that tracks model checkpoint files, architecture metadata, and attached adapters.
premises: A Model Entity contains a FileSet reference pointing to model checkpoint files (weights, config, tokenizer).
A Model Entity includes a Model Spec with auto-populated metadata about model architecture (layers, parameters).
A Model Entity tracks adapters (LoRA or other PEFT weights) attached to it and an optional base model link for fine-tuned models.

claim: An Adapter is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning artifact (e.g., LoRA weights) nested within a parent Model Entity and enabled for inference by default.
premises: Adapters are nested within the parent Model Entity and have their own FileSet for storing adapter weights.
Adapters track metadata such as fine-tuning type, rank, and alpha values.
Adapters are enabled by default post-training so NIMs serving the base model automatically load them.

claim: The NeMo Customization workflow creates a FileSet, then a Model Entity pointing to it, then a Customization Job that produces either an Adapter (LoRA) or a new Model Entity (Full SFT).
premises: Step 1: Create a FileSet with model files from HuggingFace, NGC, or local storage.
Step 2: Create a Model Entity referencing the FileSet, which auto-populates the Model Spec.
Step 3: Create a Customization Job referencing the Model Entity and dataset; LoRA creates an adapter attached to the Model Entity, Full SFT creates a new Model Entity with customized weights.

claim: LoRA training requires significantly fewer GPU resources than Full SFT, with 1-2 GPUs sufficient for models up to 13B parameters, while Full SFT requires 4-8+ GPUs.
premises: LoRA training needs 1-2 GPUs and is faster, suitable for experiments and multiple adapters per model.
Full SFT training needs 4-8+ GPUs and is slower, targeting production deployments with maximum performance.
GPU memory guidelines show LoRA minimum requirements scale from 1×16GB (1B) to 2×80GB (70B), while Full SFT scales from 1×24GB (1B) to 8+×80GB (70B).

claim: Storage requirements for customization jobs depend on training type: Full SFT needs ~3× model size, LoRA needs ~1.5×, and LoRA merged needs ~2×, excluding dataset size.
premises: Full SFT peak disk usage is ~3× model size: base model download (1×) + finetuning checkpoint (1×) + output model copy (1×).
LoRA peak disk usage is ~1.5× model size: base model download (1×) + small adapter checkpoints + adapter output.
LoRA merged peak disk usage is ~2× model size: base model download (1×) + temporary merged weights (~1×).

claim: Parallelism parameters (tensor_parallel_size, pipeline_parallel_size, context_parallel_size, expert_parallel_size) must satisfy mathematical constraints where total GPUs is a multiple of their product.
premises: Total GPUs (num_gpus_per_node × num_nodes) must be a multiple of tensor_parallel_size × pipeline_parallel_size × context_parallel_size.
data_parallel_size is automatically derived as total_gpus / (TP × PP × CP) and not set directly.
For MoE models, expert_parallel_size must evenly divide both the number of experts and the derived data_parallel_size.

claim: Adapters can be dynamically enabled or disabled on a Model Entity without deletion, with the NIM sidecar automatically reconciling adapter files within seconds.
premises: Adapters are enabled by default after training and automatically loaded by NIMs serving the base model.
Setting enabled=False causes the sidecar to remove adapter files on its next reconciliation pass (every few seconds).
Setting enabled=True causes the sidecar to re-download and serve the adapter again.

claim: NeMo Platform supports importing any HuggingFace-compatible model by creating a FileSet from a HuggingFace repo and then a Model Entity referencing that FileSet.
premises: A FileSet can be created using HuggingfaceStorageConfigParam with repo_id, repo_type, and token_secret.
A Model Entity is then created pointing to that FileSet, which auto-populates the Model Spec.
This process works for custom or proprietary models beyond the natively supported families (Llama, Nemotron, Phi, GPT-OSS).

claim: Embedding models (e.g., Llama 3.2 NV EmbedQA 1B) are supported for semantic search and RAG, while reranking models are not supported and require application-layer implementation.
premises: Embedding Models are marked as supported with use cases in semantic search, document retrieval, QA systems, and RAG pipelines.
Reranking Models are marked as not supported, with the alternative being embedding models for retrieval or application-layer reranking.
Embedding models are typically disabled by default and require administrator access.

claim: The decision framework recommends LoRA for limited GPU resources (1-2 GPUs), fast iterations, multiple use cases, or auto-deployment to existing NIMs; Full SFT for maximum performance with 4+ GPUs and production deployments.
premises: If maximum performance is needed and 4+ GPUs are available, choose Full SFT (produces new Model Entity with full weights).
Otherwise, choose LoRA; if multiple use cases, train multiple LoRA adapters on the same Model Entity; if single use case, train a single LoRA adapter.
LoRA advantages: limited GPU resources, fast training, multiple specialized versions, auto-deploy to NIMs.

claim: LLM-as-a-Judge is a technique that uses a large language model to evaluate outputs of another model based on defined criteria like helpfulness, accuracy, or tone.
premises: LLM-as-a-Judge prompts a capable LLM to score responses based on user-defined criteria.
It serves as an alternative to automated metrics or manual review for evaluating model outputs.

claim: The HelpSteer2 dataset contains approximately 10,000 prompt-response pairs with human ratings across five quality dimensions on a 0-4 scale.
premises: HelpSteer2 includes ratings for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity.
Each rating is on a 0-4 integer scale.
The dataset is used as ground truth to validate LLM judge alignment with human judgment.

claim: Creating an LLM judge metric requires defining a model, prompt template with variables, and score parsing configuration.
premises: A metric definition includes the judge model, prompt template with {{prompt}} and {{response}} placeholders, and score definition with name, range, and parser.
The tutorial uses nvidia/llama-3.3-nemotron-super-49b-v1.5 as the judge model.
Score parsing uses JsonScoreParserParam with a json_path to extract the score from the model's JSON output.

claim: Live evaluation enables synchronous testing of a metric on a few examples before running large-scale asynchronous jobs.
premises: Live evaluation runs synchronously and returns results immediately.
It is limited to 10 rows and used for quick iteration and debugging.
The tutorial tests helpfulness-v1 on two example prompt-response pairs, yielding scores of 4.0 and 0.0.

claim: Evaluation jobs process larger datasets asynchronously and produce row-level results including judge scores and ground truth for correlation analysis.
premises: Jobs are submitted via client.evaluation.metric_jobs.create with dataset, metric, and parameters like parallelism and limit_samples.
Row-level results contain original dataset items, judge requests/responses, and extracted scores.
Results are downloaded and parsed to compute Pearson r, Spearman ρ, and MAE against human annotations.

claim: Improving the prompt to align with HelpSteer2's annotation guidelines increases correlation between judge scores and human annotations.
premises: Prompt V1 is minimal ('Rate the response's helpfulness from 0-4'), while Prompt V2 includes detailed scoring criteria aligned with HelpSteer2's definition of helpfulness.
The tutorial compares both prompts by running evaluation jobs and computing correlation metrics.
The better-performing prompt (higher Pearson r) is selected for the final benchmark.

claim: Visualizing score distributions and percentiles helps diagnose judge behavior such as score clustering or miscalibration relative to human annotations.
premises: Histograms show the distribution of human and judge scores across the 0-4 range.
Percentile analysis (25th, 50th, 75th, 90th) reveals differences in score spread and central tendency.
If the judge clusters around certain values (e.g., always 3-4), the prompt may need adjustment to calibrate scoring.

claim: A benchmark combines multiple validated metrics and a dataset into a reusable evaluation suite for consistent cross-model or cross-prompt comparison.
premises: The benchmark includes the best helpfulness metric plus correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity metrics.
It is created via client.evaluation.benchmarks.create with a list of metric references and a dataset.
Benchmark jobs are run asynchronously and produce aggregate and row-level results for all dimensions.

claim: Correlation analysis across all five HelpSteer2 dimensions validates the benchmark's alignment with human judgment.
premises: Row-level benchmark results contain ground truth from the dataset and judge scores per metric.
Pearson r is computed for each dimension (helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, verbosity).
Interpretation thresholds: Strong (>0.6), Moderate (>0.4), Weak (≤0.4).

claim: Proper resource cleanup requires deleting jobs, benchmarks, metrics, filesets, and secrets before deleting the workspace due to dependency order.
premises: Workspaces cannot be deleted while containing resources.
Jobs depend on benchmarks and metrics, so they must be deleted first.
The cleanup sequence is: jobs → benchmark → metrics → fileset → secret → workspace.

claim: The quickstart.prompts module provides interactive configuration functions for quickstart setup.
premises: The module is named quickstart.prompts and described as 'Interactive prompts for quickstart configuration.'
It contains functions for detecting registry auth type, prompting for configuration, and prompting for registry credentials.

claim: The module exports specific data constants for UI symbols and registry authentication handling.
premises: The Data section lists BULLET, CHECK, CROSS, REGISTRIES_REQUIRING_AUTH, WARN, and console as module data.
These constants are presented as part of the module's public API alongside functions.

claim: Garak scores are calibrated using a bag of state-of-the-art models to estimate target model performance relative to the distribution of pass rates across surveyed models.
premises: Garak scores are interpreted compared to the state of the art using a bag of model results.
Scores from surveyed models create a distribution of possible garak scores.
A target model's pass rate is compared to the average and variation across state-of-the-art models to estimate its performance.

claim: The model bag composition follows specific criteria: quantity, recency, size diversity, provider diversity, and openness preference.
premises: The bag must have enough models for usable results but few enough for tractable experiments.
Models should be recent to avoid uncompetitive results, but not updated too frequently to maintain comparability.
Models must span size categories (1-10B, 11-99B, 100B+ parameters), no more than two from the same provider, and open weights models are preferred.

claim: Pass rates and Z-scores are calculated per probe/detector pair using mean and standard deviation across bag models, with artificial lower bounds on standard deviation.
premises: Each probe/detector pair yields a pass rate (1 - ASR) for each model in the bag.
Mean pass rate, standard deviation, and Shapiro-Wilk p-value are computed across all bag models.
Z-scores are calculated for target models; standard deviations are artificially bounded at a non-zero minimum to handle perfect agreement and represent sampling uncertainty.

claim: A high Z-score can coexist with a low absolute pass rate, and a low Z-score can coexist with a high absolute pass rate, reflecting relative rather than absolute performance.
premises: A great Z-score with a low absolute score means the target performed badly but so did other state-of-the-art models.
A low Z-score with a high absolute score means the target was not very weak, but other models were even less weak.
Z-scores measure performance relative to the bag distribution, not absolute safety.

claim: The model bag is updated between twice-yearly and quarterly to balance recency with result comparability, starting with the first benchmark in summer 2024.
premises: The first benchmark was in summer 2024.
Updates between twice-yearly and quarterly provide a good trade-off between using recent models and keeping results comparable over time.
Frequent updates make cross-run comparison difficult; infrequent updates risk uncompetitive baselines.

claim: The Winter 2026 bag contains 22 models from 15 providers, spanning parameter counts from 1.2B to 235B, with multiple models from ai21labs, ibm, meta, mistralai, nvidia, openai, and qwen.
premises: The Winter 2026 bag table lists 22 models with provider, name, and parameter count.
Providers with multiple models include ai21labs (2), ibm (2), meta (2), mistralai (2), nvidia (3), openai (2), qwen (2).
Parameter counts range from 1.2B (LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct) to 235B (llama-3_1-nemotron-ultra-253b-v1), with several models having NA parameter counts.

claim: The Spring 2025 bag contains 22 models from 14 providers, with parameter counts from 1B to 671B, and uses a reduced probe_spec with extended_detectors: false and generations: 3.
premises: The Spring 2025 bag table lists 22 models with provider, name, and parameter count.
Parameter counts range from 1B (gemma-3-27b-it listed as 1B) to 671B (deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b), with multiple models from deepseek, ibm, meta, mistralai, nvidia, qwen.
Configuration differs from Winter 2026: generations: 3, extended_detectors: false, and a shorter probe_spec list.

claim: The Summer 2024 bag contains 13 models from 11 providers, with parameter counts from 2B to 340B, and uses a probe_spec including replay and knownbadsignatures not present in later versions.
premises: The Summer 2024 bag table lists 13 models with provider, name, and parameter count.
Parameter counts range from 2B (gemma-2b) to 340B (nemotron-4-340b-instruct).
Configuration includes generations: 3, extended_detectors: false, and a probe_spec that includes replay and knownbadsignatures probes absent in Spring 2025 and Winter 2026.

claim: Bag configurations across all three snapshots share common detector settings for misleading probes, requiring CUDA for MustContradictNLI and MustRefuteClaimModel.
premises: All three bag configs (Summer 2024, Spring 2025, Winter 2026) specify detectors.misleading.MustContradictNLI.hf_args.device: cuda.
All three specify detectors.misleading.MustRefuteClaimModel.hf_args.device: cuda.
These settings are consistent despite differences in probe_spec, generations, and extended_detectors.

claim: Encoding probes across all bag configurations use the same payload sets: default, xss, and slur_terms.
premises: All three bag configs specify probes.encoding.payloads with default, xss, and slur_terms.
Summer 2024 lists them as a single string 'default,xss,slur_terms'; Spring 2025 and Winter 2026 use a YAML list format.
The payload set is unchanged across all documented bag versions.
